summary:
The poll model's design is mainstream. A hidden trend that moves as a random walk, read through polls that each carry a firm-specific lean, is the Jackman (2005) and Linzer (2013) design. The multiparty version on a log-ratio scale is Stoetzer et al. (2019) and Walther (2015). The Economist model (Heidemanns, Gelman and Morris 2020) has the same main ingredients as this model: poll-level error beyond the sampling margin, and a bias that changes over time. Centring house effects across firms is the restriction Jackman says real-time tracking needs. That is why the industry's common error has to enter at projection. Total poll error is about twice the sampling margin, and a shared bias of 1-2 points per party survives any amount of averaging (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018; Selb et al. 2023 for Germany). Israeli (Gabay 2022) and Spanish (Montalvo et al. 2019) evidence ties house effects to sponsors' politics. In Germany they are small, so Israel's large firm drifts are a local fact.

The literature backs the CLR change. A logistic-normal latent is free of the reference choice only when its covariance is unrestricted. The old latent had independent walks against the last merged block, which on today's data is Tzomet Beit Yisrael, a micro-list. That is the low-abundance reference Greenacre et al. tell analysts to avoid. With 21 lists, the reference's own innovation variance was about a twentieth of any other list's: the 'frozen reference' that s.46 measured (0.595% latent against 0.30% polls). Two refinements follow. First, the shipped CLR walk has a direction the data cannot see (the row mean). That plausibly explains the failed default-seed refit (ESS 98), and a sum-to-zero parameterisation removes it. The ALR fallback should also use a stable reference. Second, Stoetzer et al. let parties' movements covary, which would let the polls carry the within-bloc substitution that is now declared at projection.

A binomial floor with design effects declared by mode is weakly supported. The best measured design effects (UK 2015 final polls) were mostly below 1, because firms calibrate on past vote, and online panels were no worse than phone. Opt-in panels' real defect is bias (Pew 2023), which belongs in the graded precision prior. The harness's rejection of the floor agrees with Linzer. Within-firm smoothness, the s.23 symptom, is what Silver Bulletin now penalises in the rating itself (distance from the average below the sampling minimum). That points to a herding penalty in the lam prior rather than in the likelihood. Silver's record also shows past accuracy is a weak guide until about 30 graded polls. The scorecard grades at most eight final polls per firm, with light shrinkage.

Student-t errors are standard (Lange et al. 1989), but the model applies them cell by cell. A poll-level t would downweight a bad poll as a whole. Proportional treatment of undecideds is the textbook baseline (Linzer; Walsh et al.). But static allocation biases forecasts when the undecided share is large (Bon et al. 2019: 3-5% in the US against about 12% in Israel), which supports the separate measured-lean layer. Israeli law (s.16E) makes firms file results, sample size and method with the CEC. That gives the raw-share displacement a legal footing, and the displaced pairs let the model measure its seat-table conversion error directly.

findings.claim: A state-space model pools polls over a campaign: a hidden level of support that moves as a random walk, observed through polls that each add sampling error and a firm-specific bias (house effect). The pooled estimate is less biased and more precise than any single poll. Level and house effects cannot both be learned from polls alone. Jackman pinned the trajectory to the actual result, and says real-time tracking needs a priori restrictions on the house effects.
findings.quant: Australia 2004, five poll series. Measurement model y_i ~ N(a_t + d_j, s_i^2), with s_i set from each poll's n (p. 508). Two-party-preferred house effects (Table 1, p. 513): ANU/ninemsn internet poll -5.7 pp [-7.3, -4.2]; Roy Morgan (face to face) -4.9; Newspoll -2.9; ACNielsen -1.1; Galaxy +0.1 [-2.0, 1.8]. Mean of the three phone polls about -1.3 (2PP) and -0.1 (first preferences). The largest house effects track interview mode. Full text read. Venue note: Australian Journal of Political Science, not the American JPS.

source.authors: Simon Jackman
source.title: Pooling the polls over an election campaign

findings.model_link: fit(): weekly random-walk latent plus delta (firm x list house effects). delta_c is centred across firms for each list, which is the real-time restriction Jackman says is needed. So the industry-wide error cannot be learned inside the fit, and it enters at projection (correlated bloc swing, family shocks, per-list residual).
findings.site_use: The poll model follows the state-space tradition (Jackman 2005; Linzer 2013): a hidden trend, read through polls that each carry their firm's estimated lean.

findings.claim: Linzer's dynamic Bayesian model uses a binomial likelihood on decided respondents only, excludes undecideds, uses a reverse random walk, and has no house-effect terms. He argues firm-specific corrections are impractical when most firms publish few polls. He also argues that deflating sample sizes to absorb over-dispersion makes the model underestimate how much opinion moves, which worsens overconfidence in the forecast.
findings.quant: US 2008 state polls. p. 126: undecided excluded; deflating n 'worsens the problem of overconfidence'. p. 132: in a typical state, poll results varied three to five times more than the latent trend; 98% of daily latent changes were under 0.5 pp. Full text read.

source.authors: Drew A. Linzer
source.title: Dynamic Bayesian Forecasting of Presidential Elections in the States
source.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 108(501):124-134

findings.model_link: s.23 sampling floor (BAYES_FLOOR, off): the eight-cycle harness rejected a uniform binomial-times-DEFF floor (pooled MAE 1.66 -> 1.71). Linzer gives the same verdict on uniform noise inflation from US data. The mechanism differs: in this model the floor widened intervals rather than narrowing them. CEC filings renormalised to the party sum = Linzer's exclusion of undecideds.
findings.site_use: A uniform sampling-error floor was tested and did not improve the eight-cycle record; Linzer (2013) reached a similar verdict on inflating poll noise for US state polls.

findings.claim: The Economist 2020 model (Linzer lineage, in Stan) layers poll-level adjustments over a random-walk latent with correlated states. The adjustments are pollster house effects, mode (phone vs online), population (likely voters vs adults), and a time-varying partisan non-response adjustment modelled as an autoregressive process. It also has poll-level and state-level polling-error terms for measurement error beyond the stated margin of error. Priors were tuned by cross-validation on past cycles.
findings.quant: Priors started from about a 3% polling error per poll, from historical data. Innovation-sd priors were cross-validated on 2008, 2012, 2016 and early 2020 (preprint pp. 2-4). Preprint read: sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/hdsr_forecasting.pdf.

source.authors: Merlin Heidemanns; Andrew Gelman; G. Elliott Morris
source.title: An Updated Dynamic Bayesian Forecasting Model for the US Presidential Election

findings.model_link: s_obs x lam (estimated excess noise per list and firm) is the poll-level error term. The house-effect drift (s.21, linear) is a simpler cousin of their AR non-response term. The model has no explicit mode term: mode enters only through DEFF, and the floor that uses DEFF is off.
findings.site_use: Each poll is allowed error beyond its sampling margin, estimated from the data, as in the Economist model (Heidemanns, Gelman and Morris 2020).

findings.claim: The reference multiparty dynamic Bayesian model has five parts. (1) A multinomial likelihood using each poll's n. (2) An additive-log-ratio latent with the last party as baseline. (3) House effects that sum to zero across parties within each firm, and across firms. (4) A backward random walk. (5) A FULL innovation covariance W = diag(sigma) Omega diag(sigma) with an LKJ(50) prior, so parties' latent movements may covary.
findings.quant: German Bundestag 2017. sigma_j ~ N+(0, 0.1) per DAY on the log-ratio scale. Footnote 9: a 0.1 log-ratio step moves a 50% party about 2 pp, which they call a rather unusually big jump (pp. 256-257). Full text read.

source.authors: Lukas F. Stoetzer; Marcel Neunhoeffer; Thomas Gschwend; Simon Munzert; Sebastian Sternberg
source.title: Forecasting Elections in Multiparty Systems: A Bayesian Approach Combining Polls and Fundamentals

findings.model_link: Latent z. Until 15 Oct it was ALR with an independent HalfNormal(0.06) weekly tau per coordinate and no covariance. A full covariance is what makes ALR independent of the reference choice. The shipped CLR latent (s.46) is also independent per list, so it has no within-bloc covariance in the walk (Challenge 2).
findings.site_use: The latent follows the log-ratio approach used in multiparty forecasting (Stoetzer et al. 2019), which keeps every list's share between 0 and 1 and the total at 100%.

findings.claim: The Jackman dynamic linear model carries over to multiparty systems (Germany, Sweden) and gives reasonable forecasts despite system complexity and the emergence of new parties. Adding a seasonal component for cyclical swings in party support significantly lowers early-campaign forecast error.
findings.quant: Abstract read; full text not opened, so no error figures retrieved (unverified beyond the abstract).

source.authors: Daniel Walther
source.title: Picking the winner(s): Forecasting elections in multiparty systems

findings.model_link: Supports a state-space poll model for a multiparty system. Informs the campaign volatility calendar (campaign_vol_weight), a deterministic counterpart to a cyclical term.
findings.site_use: State-space poll aggregation has been tested in multiparty systems such as Germany and Sweden (Walther 2015; Stoetzer et al. 2019).

findings.claim: Across US state-level polls, total error is about twice what reported margins imply. The model writes poll variance as p(1-p)/n + tau_r^2, an additive election-level excess variance. Poll bias is alpha_r + beta_r t, an election-level bias that may change linearly in time. Firm house effects are left out of the mean, so they enter the variance. The shared bias persists however many polls are averaged.
findings.quant: 4,221 polls, 608 elections, 1998-2014, final three weeks. RMSE about 3.5 pp, about twice the error reported margins imply. Average absolute election-level bias about 2 pp: 2.1 Senate, 2.3 governor, 1.2 president (p. 613). Prior sigma_tau ~ N+(0, 0.05^2) on the logit scale (p. 611); model on p. 610. JASA-formatted PDF read (5harad.com/papers/polling-errors.pdf).

source.authors: Houshmand Shirani-Mehr; David Rothschild; Sharad Goel; Andrew Gelman
source.title: Disentangling Bias and Variance in Election Polls
source.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 113(522):607-614

findings.model_link: Industry (election-level) bias is shared by all firms and cannot be averaged away, so it lives in the projection's correlated bloc swing and family shocks. Their linear-in-time bias matches the house-effect drift (s.21). Their additive excess-variance form, binomial plus tau^2, is the template for any revived floor (Challenge 4).
findings.site_use: Polls share a common error that averaging cannot remove (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018), which is why the forecast adds an industry-wide shock on election day.

findings.claim: Applying the Shirani-Mehr model, with more temporal flexibility, to a multiparty system: German poll errors are dominated by biases common to the whole industry. Variance is about twice what margins of error imply, and there is little evidence of house or mode effects.
findings.quant: 5,240 German national polls, 1994-2021. Average absolute election-day bias per party about 1.5 pp, from 0.9 (Greens) to 3.2 (CDU/CSU). Variance about 2x nominal. Abstract read (Crossref record); full text not opened.

source.authors: Peter Selb; Sina Chen; John Körtner; Philipp Bosch
source.title: Bias and Variance in Multiparty Election Polls

findings.model_link: Supports a multiparty excess-variance term and industry shocks at projection. Contrast: the Israeli fit finds firm drifts of up to about 3 seats end to end (s.21: Tatika/Likud -2.95, Filber/UTJ -1.88). House effects are a larger share of error in Israel than in Germany, so the house-effect layer is a local necessity rather than a universal one.
findings.site_use: In multiparty systems as in two-party ones, polls vary about twice as much as their stated margins suggest (Selb et al. 2023).

findings.claim: A multilevel decomposition of Spanish poll errors has four parts: a time-invariant house effect that persists ACROSS elections, an election-level bias common to all firms, a common linear trend, and idiosyncratic error with party covariances. Estimated house effects lined up with sponsors' politics. Sigma Dos (for El Mundo) leaned to the PP, Invymark (for La Sexta) to the PSOE, and the public CIS showed none. Declared margins of error understated the true uncertainty.
findings.quant: 157 polls within 30 days of the 1996-2011 Congressional elections. In one cycle, firms collectively missed the PSOE-PP differential by 7 pp. arXiv version (1612.03073) read, pp. 9-10 and 14-15.

source.authors: José G. Montalvo; Omiros Papaspiliopoulos; Timothée Stumpf-Fétizon
source.title: Bayesian forecasting of electoral outcomes with new parties' competition

findings.model_link: Here, house effects are re-learned inside each 240-day window from a zero-mean group prior, and only firm PRECISION carries over from past cycles (the lam scorecard). Montalvo et al. carry the signed lean across elections too (Challenge 7).
findings.site_use: new claim

findings.claim: Across the three 2019-20 Israeli elections, media-sponsored polls were biased in line with the sponsoring outlet's stance on Netanyahu. Polls commissioned by anti-Netanyahu outlets consistently underestimated the seats the pro-Netanyahu bloc won.
findings.quant: Bias defined as a systematic over- or under-estimate of the pro-Netanyahu bloc's seats. Abstract read; per-outlet magnitudes not retrieved (unverified).

source.authors: Nadav Gabay
source.title: The effect of news media political bias on pre-elections poll results: evidence from the 2019-20 Israeli elections

findings.model_link: Israeli evidence for firm/sponsor house effects (delta; correlation groups in pollster_meta.csv), and for leans at the BLOC level rather than list by list. The firm-level delta absorbs sponsor effects only where each firm has one sponsor.
findings.site_use: Israeli research finds that poll bias tracks the commissioning outlet's politics (Gabay 2022), which is why each firm carries its own estimated lean.

findings.claim: Israeli law requires anyone who conducts an election poll for publication or broadcast to send the Central Elections Committee a copy of the results. The filing must state the sampling method, initial sample size, populations sampled, how many people were asked, took part, refused or were ineligible, the interview dates and hours, and the margin of error. The CEC posts filings as received.
findings.quant: Elections (Modes of Propaganda) Law, 5719-1959, s. 16E(e)(1)-(3) (Hebrew s. 16ה; consolidated text updated to 8 Aug 2022, published by the CEC on gov.il). In 2026 the pipeline parsed 103 filings (brief); 74 were merged at the 13 Oct refit (s.41). Official text read.

source.authors: State of Israel (Knesset); text published by the Central Elections Committee
source.title: Elections (Modes of Propaganda) Law, 5719-1959, section 16E (election polls) - consolidated text

findings.model_link: _merge_cec: filed raw shares displace seat-derived table numbers. Filing n feeds n_resp, and the filed undecided share feeds u_c (beta_u) and the undecided pool (U_POOL). The method and response fields are an untapped source for firm-level design information (Challenge 4).
findings.site_use: Where a firm's legal filing to the Central Elections Committee gives raw percentages, those replace numbers reverse-engineered from its published seat table.

findings.claim: Polls are not independent. In the 2012 Republican primaries, automated (IVR) polls were as accurate as live-interviewer polls when a traditional poll had already been published in the state, and markedly worse when none had. That suggests pollsters take cues from each other. If so, a poll of polls is misleadingly precise.
findings.quant: 159 polls released after the 2012 New Hampshire primary. Overall IVR-vs-human difference -0.256 (n.s.). IVR polls with no prior human poll in the state had an average absolute error 3.229 points larger (p. 335). Authors call it suggestive, not conclusive. Full text read.

source.authors: Joshua D. Clinton; Steven Rogers
source.title: Robo-Polls: Taking Cues from Traditional Sources?

findings.model_link: The likelihood treats polls as conditionally independent given the latent and house effects. Herding was measured (dossier s.12: final-window dispersion 0.88x mid-campaign, 0.6-0.9x sampling noise) and deliberately left out to avoid double counting with the backtest-calibrated shocks. Effective sample size is still overstated inside the fit (Challenge 5).
findings.site_use: Pollsters partly follow one another, so twenty polls carry less information than twenty independent samples (Clinton and Rogers 2013).

findings.claim: US state presidential polls in 2000-2008 did not behave like random samples. Standardised errors against the result were far more dispersed than sampling theory implies, and they were biased. Treating undecided respondents as ignorable (dropping them proportionally) removed most of the raw shortfall. The authors suggest pollsters may avoid publishing 'atypical' polls. NOTE for the brief: this paper documents OVER-dispersion against the outcome, not panel smoothness. It does not support the s.23 stickiness diagnosis.
findings.quant: Table 1, N = 1,857 polls. Variance of standardised errors 1.58-4.38, against 1 under random sampling. Raw Republican error -3.48 pp becomes 0.03 after the undecided adjustment; Democratic -4.57 becomes -1.04. Polls picked the wrong state winner 18-20% of the time. Author-hosted AEA Papers & Proceedings version read.

source.authors: Elias Walsh; Sarah Dolfin; John DiNardo
source.title: Lies, Damn Lies, and Pre-Election Polling

findings.model_link: Supports proportional renormalisation of filings (raw_pct / party sum) as the baseline undecided treatment, and an estimated excess-variance term. It is NOT evidence for a floor driven by panel smoothness.
findings.site_use: new claim

findings.claim: A pollster's accuracy is only modestly predictable. Past accuracy correlates with future accuracy, but a firm's record is mostly noise until it has about 30 graded polls. The best firms are about 1 point better than average. Methodology and transparency standards predict accuracy and serve as the prior that records are shrunk toward.
findings.quant: Average poll missed the result by 5.3 points. Correlation of past with future accuracy, 1998-2007 vs 2008 on: about 0.6 (simple average error), about 0.45 (Advanced Plus-Minus). Firms in the AAPOR Transparency Initiative, NCPP or the Roper archive averaged 4.6 vs 5.5 points of error (1998-2009) and 4.0 vs 5.2 out of sample (2012). The 25 Sept 2014 article now redirects; its text was read via the author's syndicated copy (goodreads.com/author_blog_posts/7073023).

source.authors: Nate Silver
source.title: How FiveThirtyEight Calculates Pollster Ratings

findings.model_link: lam prior from the 8-cycle scorecard. q is shrunk to the industry median by n_cycles/(n_cycles+3), and only the FINAL pre-election poll per cycle is graded (s.23). That is at most 8 graded polls per firm, far below the ~30 at which 538 lets a record dominate. A firm with 8 cycles keeps 73% of its own record (Challenge 6).
findings.site_use: Firm weights lean on their graded record, shrunk toward the industry average, because past accuracy predicts future accuracy only weakly (Silver 2014).

findings.claim: The current Silver Bulletin pollster ratings penalise herding directly. If a firm's Average Distance from the Polling Average (ADPA) is below the theoretical minimum implied by its polls' sampling error, a penalty is added to its accuracy score before the predictive rating is computed. Ratings are mean-reverted by number of polls, with older polls discounted, and transparency earns a bonus.
findings.quant: January 2026 update (14 Jan 2026), read. The page does not state the penalty or bonus sizes.

source.authors: Nate Silver; Eli McKown-Dawson
source.title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings (January 2026 update)

findings.model_link: s.23 found this symptom within firms: NB-bloc scatter around each firm's own trend was 0.43-0.67 seats, against a binomial 2-3 seats. The fix tried was a likelihood floor, which the harness rejected. An ADPA-type herding penalty on the lam PRIOR is the ratings-side alternative (Challenge 5).
findings.site_use: new claim

findings.claim: Bootstrap design effects for the 2015 UK final polls were mostly BELOW 1. Calibrating on past vote or party identification, which correlate strongly with current vote intention, made the estimates more efficient than simple random sampling. Without those variables, design effects were 1.04-1.68. Online opt-in panels did not show larger design effects than phone polls. The miss itself, a Conservative lead underestimated by about 7 points, came from unrepresentative samples: a shared bias, not variance.
findings.quant: Table 2, d2 (Con/Lab). Online panels 0.42-1.17: Opinium 0.42/0.47, YouGov 0.76/0.76, Panelbase 1.17/1.16. Phone 0.53-1.40: ICM 0.53/0.68, Ipsos-MORI 1.37/1.40. Without past-vote/party-ID calibration, 1.04-1.68. Accepted manuscript read (ora.ox.ac.uk).

source.authors: Patrick Sturgis; Jouni Kuha; Nick Baker; Mario Callegaro; Stephen Fisher; Jane Green; Will Jennings; Benjamin E. Lauderdale; Patten Smith
source.title: An assessment of the causes of the errors in the 2015 UK general election opinion polls
source.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 181(3):757-781

findings.model_link: DEFF table (phone 1.0, mixed 1.1, opt-in online 1.3, SMS 1.4) is declared, not measured, and the best measured evidence does not order modes that way. s.23 also computed within-firm scatter on the NB-BLOC total, the quantity that past-vote calibration makes most stable, so some sub-binomial smoothness may be design efficiency, not stickiness (Challenge 4).
findings.site_use: new claim

findings.claim: Across 28 benchmarks, online opt-in samples had about twice the error of probability-based panels. The excess was concentrated among young and Hispanic adults and traced to bogus respondents. It is a bias problem, not a sampling-variance problem.
findings.quant: Average absolute error 5.8 points for opt-in (three vendors: 6.4, 6.1, 5.0) vs 2.6 for probability panels (2.3, 3.0, 2.5). Ages 18-29: 11.2 vs 3.6; Hispanic adults: 10.8 vs 3.6. Six samples, 29,937 adults, June-July 2021. Report page read.

source.authors: Andrew Mercer; Arnold Lau
source.title: Comparing Two Types of Online Survey Samples

findings.model_link: Opt-in panel quality belongs in the precision prior (graded record, lam) and in house effects, not in a variance-only design effect. This backs the shipped choice of letting the graded record carry firm quality.
findings.site_use: Online opt-in panels carry more error than probability samples (Pew Research Center 2023), so each firm's weight rests on its graded record rather than on its sample size.

findings.claim: The AAPOR task force holds that the margin of sampling error does not apply to non-probability samples, and that precision there is a model-based quantity. Replicate-sample methods estimate variance but cannot detect bias. Treating such estimates as having no error is not acceptable either.
findings.quant: Full task-force report, pp. 82-83 (summary in JSSAM 1(2):90-143). Report read (aapor.org PDF).

source.authors: Reg Baker; J. Michael Brick; Nancy A. Bates; Mike Battaglia; Mick P. Couper; Jill A. Dever; Krista J. Gile; Roger Tourangeau
source.title: Summary Report of the AAPOR Task Force on Non-probability Sampling
source.venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 1(2):90-143

findings.model_link: Supports estimating each list's and firm's noise from the data (s_obs, lam) rather than imposing sqrt(p(1-p)/n x DEFF) on opt-in panels as if they were probability samples.
findings.site_use: For opt-in panels a textbook margin of error does not apply (AAPOR 2013); the model estimates each firm's noise from its record instead.

findings.claim: Static allocation of undecided respondents, proportional or even, biased 2016 US polls and poll aggregates. Undecideds did not split in proportion to decided voters, and a probabilistic allocation that carries its own uncertainty does better. The problem grows with the undecided share.
findings.quant: Weighted mean undecided in the final week: 5.1% (2016), 3.5% (2012), 3.9% (2008), 2.7% (2004). For comparison, Israel 2026's pool is about 12% of the electorate (U_POOL from CEC filings; N12 30 Jul, n 505). Accepted manuscript read.

source.authors: Joshua J. Bon; Timothy Ballard; Bernard Baffour
source.title: Polling bias and undecided voter allocations: US presidential elections, 2004-2016
source.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 182(2):467-493

findings.model_link: Filed shares are renormalised proportionally (_merge_cec), beta_u widens noise for high-undecided polls, and the projection's measured undecided-lean layer (U_LEAN_PER_SIDE, Beta posterior) is a probabilistic allocation. Backs keeping that layer separate from the poll fit.
findings.site_use: Undecided voters are not assumed to split like decided ones: the forecast draws their lean from measured data, with its own uncertainty (cf. Bon, Ballard and Baffour 2019).

findings.claim: Replacing normal errors with Student-t errors gives robust likelihood-based inference. The degrees of freedom are a convenient robustness setting that can be estimated or fixed. In the multivariate t, one scale-mixing factor is shared by all components of an observation, so an aberrant observation is downweighted as a whole.
findings.quant: Abstract read via a bibliographic mirror. The common 'df = 4' default attributed to this paper is NOT verified.

source.authors: Kenneth L. Lange; Roderick J. A. Little; Jeremy M. G. Taylor
source.title: Robust Statistical Modeling Using the t Distribution
source.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 84(408):881-896

findings.model_link: StudentT(nu=4) likelihood, applied independently to each poll x list cell on the share scale.
findings.site_use: The poll likelihood is fat-tailed (Student-t), so one aberrant number cannot drag the trend (Lange, Little and Taylor 1989).

findings.claim: A logratio Student-t distribution puts heavy tails inside the simplex geometry. It is equivalent across logratio representations for estimation and outlier detection, and it flags outlying whole compositions better than classical robust methods.
findings.quant: Monte Carlo under scale contamination, with a leave-one-out procedure: higher AUC and near-perfect specificity against MCD and COMCoDa. Abstract read; full text not opened.

source.authors: Gianna Serafina Monti; Gloria Mateu-Figueras; Vera Pawlowsky-Glahn; Juan José Egozcue
source.title: The logratio Student's t distribution: a robust model for compositional data analysis

findings.model_link: The model's t is applied per list cell. A poll that is wrong as a whole (a mis-parsed filing, a different question, a composite list) is downweighted cell by cell, not coherently, and the cells it does not downweight still pull the latent (Challenge 3).
findings.site_use: new claim

findings.claim: The logistic-normal family is closed under permutation of parts, as Aitchison (1986) proved: reordering the parts transforms (mu, Sigma) linearly. So the family is reference-free only when Sigma is unrestricted. A diagonal Sigma (independent coordinates) under one reference is generally not diagonal under another. Independent random walks per ALR coordinate are therefore a reference-specific assumption.
findings.quant: Property 7, p. 12: Sigma_P = (U'PU) Sigma (U'P'U). p. 14: closure under permutation and subcompositions of the logistic normal, proved by Aitchison (1986). arXiv full text read. Own derivation for the old latent (D = 21, equal tau): the reference list's centred-log-ratio innovation variance is (D-1)/D^2 tau^2 = 0.045 tau^2, against [(D-1)^2+(D-2)]/D^2 tau^2 = 0.95 tau^2 for every other list (sd ratio 0.22).

source.authors: Gloria Mateu-Figueras; Vera Pawlowsky-Glahn; Juan José Egozcue
source.title: The normal distribution in some constrained sample spaces

findings.model_link: Backs the CLR latent shipped 15 Oct (s.46). The ALR latent's reference was the last merged block; on today's data prepare_data() makes it 'beit_yisrael'. Its implied volatility was about a twentieth of any other list's. The refit moved Tzomet Beit Yisrael from 0.595% to 0.339%, toward its 0.30% polls (s.46): the 'frozen reference' measured.
findings.site_use: The latent treats every list symmetrically (centred log-ratios), so no list's movement depends on which list happens to be the reference.

findings.claim: An additive-log-ratio transformation can come measurably close to the full (isometric) logratio geometry if the reference part is well chosen. The first criterion is high Procrustes correlation with the exact geometry, the second is low variance of the log reference, and references with low abundance or many zeros should be avoided.
findings.quant: Procrustes correlations of 0.9991, 0.9974 and 0.9902 on three datasets with the chosen references. Full text read.

source.authors: Michael Greenacre; Marina Martínez-Álvaro; Agustín Blasco
source.title: Compositional Data Analysis of Microbiome and Any-Omics Datasets: A Validation of the Additive Logratio Transformation

findings.model_link: The old ALR reference, a micro-list polled in few polls (MIN_LIST_POLLS = 3), was exactly the low-abundance, high-noise reference to avoid. The ALR path is still live: it is the refit-gate FALLBACK when CLR fails twice (s.46) and the research latent under BAYES_CLR=0. Its reference should be fixed to a large, stable list (Challenge 1).
findings.site_use: new claim

findings.claim: Aitchison's pairwise and additive logratios are quasi-isometric in practice; exact isometry is not a prerequisite for good analysis. With a near-constant reference (geochemists use silica, the most abundant and stable part), ALRs behave like logs of their numerators. The centred log-ratio is the symmetric alternative: logs taken against the geometric mean, which sum to zero (D-1 free dimensions) and preserve all pairwise logratio distances.
findings.quant: Sections 3.3-3.4 (arXiv 2201.05197, pp. 4-5). Full text read.

source.authors: Michael Greenacre; Eric Grunsky; John Bacon-Shone; Ionas Erb; Thomas Quinn

findings.claim: PyMC provides a Normal distribution constrained to sum to zero along an axis, N(0, sigma^2 (I_K - J_K/K)), which has exactly K-1 free directions. Sigma must be shared across the constrained axis.
findings.quant: Documentation for pymc.ZeroSumNormal (stable docs, read 15 Oct 2026); n_zerosum_axes defaults to 1.

source.title: pymc.ZeroSumNormal (API documentation)

findings.model_link: The shipped CLR walk draws B free z0/steps and row-centres afterwards, so the row mean is a direction the likelihood cannot see. s.46: the default-seed CLR refit failed the gates (max r-hat 1.04, min ESS 98), and two harness windows showed bimodal endpoint shares attributed to that common-mode direction. A sum-to-zero parameterisation removes it (Challenge 1).

findings.claim: Unequal weights alone inflate the variance of a weighted mean by deffK = 1 + relvariance(w), the Kish design effect. The formula assumes weights unrelated to the outcome. Calibration on variables that predict the outcome can push the true design effect below 1 (cf. AGG-F15).
findings.quant: Formula and citations read in the PracTools R documentation (deffK), which cites Kish (1965) Survey Sampling and Kish (1992). The 1992 paper itself was NOT opened (unverified beyond the formula).

source.authors: Leslie Kish
source.title: Weighting for unequal Pi

findings.model_link: The declared DEFF values (1.0-1.4) are in the range Kish's formula gives for moderately weighted samples, but heavily weighted opt-in panels can exceed them and past-vote calibration can undercut them. A firm-specific value should come from filed weights or from the data, not from mode.

challenges.title: CLR is right; finish the job: no unidentified direction, and a stable reference for the ALR fallback
challenges.what_literature_says: A logistic-normal latent is reference-free only with an unrestricted covariance (Aitchison; Mateu-Figueras et al.). Independent ALR walks are reference-specific, and the ALR reference should be abundant and stable (Greenacre et al. 2021, 2023). CLR coordinates sum to zero and have D-1 free dimensions, and PyMC's ZeroSumNormal implements exactly that.
challenges.current_model: Shipped 15 Oct (s.46): CLR with B free z0/tau/steps, row-centred after the cumulative sum. The row mean is unidentified by the data. The default-seed refit failed (r-hat 1.04, ESS 98) and the reseed passed (ESS 395); two harness windows showed bimodal endpoint shares. The fallback (gate failure) and research path (BAYES_CLR=0) is ALR against the last merged block: today 'beit_yisrael', a micro-list.
challenges.proposed_change: (a) Draw z0 and each week's innovations in the sum-to-zero subspace. Either eps ~ ZeroSumNormal(1) or an orthonormal (Helmert/ILR) basis times N(0, I_{B-1}), then multiply by the per-list tau and re-centre; or use ZeroSumNormal(tau) if a common tau is acceptable. The latent then has B-1 free directions per step and keeps CLR's symmetry. (b) In the ALR fallback, fix the reference to the largest, most-polled list (Likud) instead of merge order.
challenges.how_to_test: Refit gates on 2026 data at 5 seeds: divergences, max r-hat, bulk ESS, holdout. Success means no reseed is needed and every seed passes. Harness: a CLR-fidelity arm with the reparameterisation must reproduce the clr_latent record (eve 1.509/1.628/.981/.0474) within seed noise. For (b), run an ALR-fallback arm with the Likud reference vs merge-order reference.

challenges.title: Let the latent carry within-bloc substitution (innovation covariance)
challenges.what_literature_says: The reference multiparty model estimates a full innovation covariance W = diag(sigma) Omega diag(sigma) with an LKJ(50) prior, so parties' movements can covary (Stoetzer et al. 2019). Independent walks rule that out a priori.
challenges.current_model: Independent per-list walks (CLR). Measured within-bloc churn (Yashar <-> Together/Democrats; Midgam 27 Jul) enters only at projection as a DECLARED zero-sum exchange (CENTRE_CHURN) and through the certainty layer.
challenges.proposed_change: Add a low-rank correlation to the CLR innovations, either a bloc factor or LKJ on a reduced set of large lists. The posterior then learns substitution from the 2026 polls, and CENTRE_CHURN is switched off in that arm to avoid double counting.
challenges.how_to_test: Harness at D-21 and D-56, where the forward walk matters. Compare list MAE, bloc Brier and the interval score against clr_latent. Check the posterior correlation between Yashar and Together innovations on 2026 data against the declared churn.

challenges.title: Robustness at the poll level, not the cell level
challenges.what_literature_says: The t distribution's robustness comes from a scale-mixing factor. In the multivariate t, an aberrant observation is downweighted as a whole (Lange et al. 1989). For compositions, a logratio t detects outlying whole compositions (Monti et al. 2026).
challenges.current_model: StudentT(nu=4) applied independently to each poll x list share. A poll that is wrong as a whole (a mis-parsed CEC filing, a composite list, a different question) is downweighted only in its most extreme cells. Its other cells still pull the latent.
challenges.proposed_change: Add a poll-level scale mixture: one w_p ~ InvGamma(nu/2, nu/2) per poll multiplies that poll's sigma for all its lists, with nu estimated (or kept at 4), keeping a mild per-cell t if needed.
challenges.how_to_test: Harness arm vs clr_latent (eve, D-7, D-21). Posterior predictive check: do known bad inputs (the excluded S.M.L.T. row, the 2021 composite Arab polls) get small w_p when re-admitted?

challenges.title: Design effects: measure, do not declare by mode; and recheck the stickiness diagnosis per list
challenges.what_literature_says: Total poll variance is about 2x simple random sampling (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018; Selb et al. 2023), modelled as binomial plus an estimated additive tau^2. Yet the best measured PURE sampling design effects (UK 2015 final polls) were 0.42-1.40, mostly below 1, because firms calibrate on past vote. Online panels were not worse than phone (Sturgis et al. 2018). Opt-in panels' main defect is bias, not variance (Pew 2023), and a margin of error is not defined for them (AAPOR 2013).
challenges.current_model: The floor uses sqrt(p(1-p)/n x DEFF) with DEFF declared by mode (1.0 phone to 1.4 SMS). It is OFF after the harness rejected it (s.23). The panel-stickiness diagnosis was computed on the NB-bloc total, the quantity past-vote calibration stabilises most.
challenges.proposed_change: If the floor is revisited: (i) use the Shirani-Mehr additive form, sigma^2 = c x p(1-p)/n + tau_f^2, with c estimated (a prior centred below 1 is allowed) and tau_f per firm, instead of declared mode DEFFs. (ii) Recompute within-firm scatter per list, not on the bloc total, before concluding stickiness. (iii) Read firm sampling methods from the s.16E(e)(2) CEC filing fields.
challenges.how_to_test: Own measurement first: within-firm per-list residual sd vs binomial, by firm. Then a harness arm with the estimated-c floor vs clr_latent; the shipping rule decides.

challenges.title: Price herding in the rating prior, not the likelihood
challenges.what_literature_says: Pollsters take cues from each other (Clinton and Rogers 2013). Silver Bulletin penalises firms whose distance from the polling average falls below the minimum their sampling error implies, inside the predictive rating (Silver and McKown-Dawson 2026).
challenges.current_model: Herding was measured (s.12) and kept out to avoid double counting with the backtest-calibrated shocks. The stickiness symptom (s.23) was attacked with a likelihood floor, which was rejected. The lam prior uses the graded record only.
challenges.proposed_change: Compute each firm's ADPA (mean distance from the contemporaneous average of other firms) per historical cycle against its sampling minimum. Firms below the minimum get their lam prior median multiplied by a factor, for example by inflating their prior noise in proportion to the shortfall. An alternative is a within-firm AR(1) error term, so a smooth series is not read as many independent confirmations.
challenges.how_to_test: Harness arm (leave-one-cycle-out: the ADPA penalty is computed from the training cycles only). Pre-register the penalty form. Grade on eve/D-7/D-21 against the restated CLR-fidelity baseline.

challenges.title: Grade more polls per firm and calibrate the shrinkage
challenges.what_literature_says: Past accuracy predicts future accuracy only modestly (correlation 0.45-0.6), and a record is noise-dominated until about 30 graded polls. Ratings adjust each poll's error for days to the election and revert to a methodology/transparency prior (Silver 2014; Silver Bulletin 2026).
challenges.current_model: The scorecard grades ONE poll per firm per cycle (the last before election day, exit polls excluded). q is shrunk by n_cycles/(n_cycles+3), lam ~ LogNormal(log 1/q^2, 0.20). A firm with 8 cycles keeps 73% weight on 8 graded polls.
challenges.proposed_change: Grade every poll in the final 2-3 weeks before the blackout, with a days-to-election adjustment fitted on the pooled record. Choose the shrinkage constant k by leave-one-cycle-out, from k in {3, 8, 15, 30} polls-equivalent. Consider a transparency prior: complete CEC filings with n, undecided share and method.
challenges.how_to_test: Harness arms per k (the scorecard rebuilt inside each fold from training cycles only). Metrics: median/mean MAE, coverage, Brier; also the rank stability of firm q across folds.

challenges.title: Carry signed house effects across cycles (and test sponsor grouping)
challenges.what_literature_says: Spanish house effects persist across elections and align with sponsors' politics (Montalvo et al. 2019). Israeli media-sponsored polls in 2019-20 were biased in the sponsor's direction (Gabay 2022). But in Germany house effects are small (Selb et al. 2023).
challenges.current_model: delta ~ N(gamma_group, sigma_f), zero-mean group prior, re-learned in each 240-day window. Only firm precision (lam) carries over from past cycles.
challenges.proposed_change: First measure the cycle-to-cycle correlation of each firm's (centred) per-list or per-bloc house effect, 2009-2022. If it is material, give delta a prior mean equal to the firm's previous-cycle effect times a shrink factor estimated in the harness. Test sponsor-based correlation groups as an alternative to firm groups.
challenges.how_to_test: Own measurement: correlation of house effects across consecutive cycles (lists matched by lineage). Then a harness arm with the informed prior. This matters most at D-21/D-56, when windows are thin.

challenges.title: Give seat-table-derived observations their own noise
challenges.what_literature_says: The reference aggregators fit raw shares with each poll's n: binomial in Linzer and Jackman, multinomial in Stoetzer. A published seat table is a processed product. It is rounded to whole seats, censored at the threshold, and carries the firm's own undecided allocation. Israeli filings give the raw shares (s.16E).
challenges.current_model: Table-derived shares (seats/120 x (1 - wasted - 0.01)) and filed raw shares enter with the same sig_model. Integer rounding alone adds sd 1/sqrt(12) = 0.29 seat, about 0.24 pp per list (own derivation), which is large relative to a 3-4 seat list's signal.
challenges.proposed_change: Estimate a multiplier (or an additive rounding variance) for table-derived observations. Measure it directly from the displaced pairs: each filing that displaces a table poll gives both versions of the same survey.
challenges.how_to_test: 2026-only: filings exist only for 2026, so this is not harness-testable. Measure the table-vs-filing discrepancy over the displaced pairs, then compare the 14-day holdout and posterior predictive coverage with and without the source term.

parameters.name: Latent coordinates
parameters.current: CLR (shipped 15 Oct, s.46): B independent per-list walks, row-centred; ALR fallback against the last merged block (today beit_yisrael)
parameters.literature_range: ALR with full covariance (Stoetzer et al.); ALR with an abundant, stable reference (Greenacre et al.); symmetric CLR/ILR with D-1 free directions (Aitchison; Greenacre et al. 2023)

parameters.name: Random-walk innovation scale prior
parameters.current: tau ~ HalfNormal(0.06) per list per WEEK on the log-ratio scale (x sqrt(dt))
parameters.literature_range: Stoetzer et al.: sigma_j ~ N+(0, 0.1) per DAY on the ALR scale (about 0.26 per week if daily steps are independent); Economist: cross-validated on past cycles

parameters.name: Innovation correlation across lists
parameters.current: none (independent walks); within-bloc churn declared at projection
parameters.literature_range: LKJ(50) prior on a full correlation matrix (Stoetzer et al.)

parameters.name: Likelihood tails
parameters.current: Student-t, nu = 4 fixed, independent per poll x list cell
parameters.literature_range: t with nu estimated or fixed (Lange et al.); poll-level / logratio multivariate t (Monti et al. 2026)

parameters.name: Excess poll variance
parameters.current: s_obs ~ HalfNormal(0.012) per list x lam x noise_mult x exp(beta_u u_c); binomial floor OFF
parameters.literature_range: total variance about 2x SRS (Shirani-Mehr; Selb); additive tau^2 with sigma_tau ~ N+(0, 0.05^2) on the logit scale (Shirani-Mehr); about 3% polling error per poll as a starting prior (Economist)

parameters.name: Design effect by mode (research floor only)
parameters.literature_range: bootstrap d2 0.42-1.40 for 2015 UK final polls (online 0.42-1.17, phone 0.53-1.40); 1.04-1.68 without past-vote calibration (Sturgis et al.); weighting alone 1 + relvar(w) (Kish)

parameters.name: House-effect time variation
parameters.current: linear drift per firm x list, sigma_slope ~ HalfNormal(0.01) share, centred across firms (posterior 0.0085)
parameters.literature_range: linear-in-time election-level bias (Shirani-Mehr); AR process for partisan non-response (Economist); common linear trend (Montalvo et al.)

parameters.name: House-effect identification and memory
parameters.current: centred across firms per list; no per-firm sum-to-zero across lists; zero-mean group prior re-learned each window
parameters.literature_range: sum to zero across firms (Jackman's real-time restriction); also across parties within firm (Stoetzer et al.); persistent across elections (Montalvo et al.)

parameters.name: Pollster-rating shrinkage
parameters.current: q -> industry median by n_cycles/(n_cycles+3); one graded (final, non-exit) poll per firm per cycle; lam LogNormal sigma 0.20
parameters.literature_range: record noise-dominated until about 30 graded polls; past/future accuracy correlation 0.45-0.6 (Silver 2014); mean reversion by poll count with older polls discounted (Silver Bulletin 2026)

parameters.name: Undecided treatment in the fit
parameters.current: filed shares renormalised to the party sum (proportional); beta_u ~ HalfNormal(3) widens noise with the filed undecided share; lean applied at projection
parameters.literature_range: proportional exclusion is the textbook baseline (Linzer; Walsh et al.); static allocation biases forecasts when undecideds are many; probabilistic allocation preferred (Bon et al.: US final week 2.7-5.1% vs Israel about 12%)

parameters.name: Herding adjustment
parameters.current: none in the fit or ratings (measured: final-window dispersion 0.88x mid-campaign, s.12)
parameters.literature_range: ADPA below the sampling minimum is penalised in the rating (Silver Bulletin); IVR polls with no prior human poll had +3.2 points absolute error (Clinton and Rogers)

parameters.name: Seat-table rounding noise
parameters.literature_range: integer rounding sd 1/sqrt(12) = 0.29 seat, about 0.24 pp per list (own derivation); the reference models use raw shares with n

open_questions: Jacob Shamir (1986), 'Preelection Polls in Israel: Structural Constraints on Accuracy', Public Opinion Quarterly 50(1):62-75 (doi 10.1086/268959): the only Israel-specific methodological paper on poll accuracy located. It was not opened (no abstract online); worth library access for its structural arguments.
Gabay (2022): the per-outlet magnitudes, and whether a sponsor effect survives once firm effects are in. Most Israeli firms poll for one main outlet, so firm and sponsor are nearly confounded.

Do Israeli firms weight on past (2022) vote? If so, sub-binomial within-firm scatter is partly genuine design efficiency (Sturgis et al.). The CEC filing fields required by s.16E(e)(2) (sampling method, response counts) could answer this firm by firm.

Is the shipped CLR latent's non-identified row mean the cause of the default-seed refit failure (ESS 98) and the bimodal harness endpoints? The sum-to-zero reparameterisation in Challenge 1 is the direct test.

sigma_g (group house-effect scale) mixes poorly at harness draw counts (r-hat 1.07-1.79, s.46) under both latents. A non-centred parameterisation of gamma/delta is the standard remedy; not researched here (the EVAL desk covers HMC diagnostics).

Per-firm sum-to-zero across lists (Stoetzer et al.'s identification) is not imposed. Does a firm's total lean absorb the seat-table conversion constant (the 0.01 in implied_share_obs) or unreported small lists?

The literature's synthetic models (Linzer; Stoetzer et al.; Heidemanns et al.) anchor election day on a fundamentals prior; this model has none. At D-12 those models are poll-dominated too. Whether a lineage-based prior helps first-cycle lists is open.

Coverage gaps (the shared web-search budget ran out mid-desk): Kang and Oh (2024), 'Forecasting South Korea's presidential election via multiparty dynamic Bayesian modeling', IJF 40(1):124-141 (doi 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2023.01.004). It is a compositional / Hilbert-space multiparty model, and only its abstract fragments were seen. Pasek (2015), 'Predicting Elections: Considering Tools to Pool the Polls', POQ 79(2):594-619 (doi 10.1093/poq/nfu060), and Egozcue et al. (2003), the ILR paper (doi 10.1023/A:1023818214614), were located but not opened.
